content.body: Imagine you're a quality tester at a software company. All versions are released in order, but at some point, a bug was introduced. Your job is to find the first bad version as quickly as possible. We'll learn how to solve this efficiently using a clever search technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply binary search to find the first bad version.
• Implement the solution using a while loop and midpoint calculation.
• Explain why binary search is more efficient than checking every version.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start small. You have 5 versions. Version 3 is the first bad one (all later versions are also bad). How would you find it?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: Which version is the first bad one?
content.successMessage: Correct! Version 3 is the first bad version.

content.title: Try a bigger set
content.prompt: Now with 8 versions, where version 5 is first bad. How would you find it?
content.successMessage: Well done! You likely checked from the start until you found the bad version.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: With 12 versions where version 8 is first bad. How would you approach it?
content.successMessage: Great! You checked versions sequentially until you found the first bad one.

content.body: What you just did was a linear scan: you checked each version from the beginning until you found the first bad one. That works for small numbers of versions.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When there are 10,000 versions, checking each one from the start is too slow. We need a smarter method that eliminates many versions at once. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen: we know that once we find a bad version, all later versions are also bad. We can use this property to cut our search space in half each time, rather than checking every single version.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Like finding a word in a dictionary - you don't start at page 1; you open to the middle and eliminate half the book based on whether you went too far or not far enough.

content.body: We'll use binary search: start with the entire range, check the middle version, and based on whether it's good or bad, eliminate half of the remaining versions. Repeat until we find the exact point where good turns to bad.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Example with versions 1-8, first bad is 5:
1. Check middle (4) → Good → eliminate versions 1-4
2. Check middle of 5-8 (6) → Bad → eliminate versions 7-8
3. Check middle of 5-6 (5) → Bad → found first bad version

content.body:
1. Set left = 1, right = n (total versions)
2. While left < right:
   • Calculate mid = left + Math.floor((right-left)/2)
   • If mid is bad: first bad is at mid or earlier → move right to mid
   • If mid is good: first bad is after mid → move left to mid+1
3. When left == right, that's the first bad version
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the search boundaries
steps.instruction: Initialize the left and right pointers for our binary search. Left should start at 1 (first version) and right at n (last version).
steps.hint: Remember: versions are numbered from 1 to n inclusive.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should declare two variables: left and right.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the initial search range.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you initialize both left and right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try initializing 'let left = 1' and 'let right = n'.

steps.title: Create the search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as left is less than right. This is the core of binary search.
steps.hint: We want to keep searching while there's still a range to check.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The loop will run until we've narrowed down to one version.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your condition is 'left < right'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add 'while (left < right) { }' to continue searching while there's a range.

steps.title: Calculate the midpoint
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the midpoint. Use Math.floor to ensure we get an integer. The formula is: mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2).
steps.hint: We use this formula instead of (left+right)/2 to avoid potential overflow with large numbers.
steps.expectedOutcome: Declare 'let mid' and calculate it using the given formula.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Calculating the midpoint correctly is key to binary search.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your formula. It should be 'left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add 'let mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2);' inside the loop.

steps.title: Update boundaries based on result
steps.instruction: Check if the midpoint version is bad using the provided isBadVersion(mid) function. If it's bad, move right to mid. If it's good, move left to mid + 1. Finally, return left when the loop ends.
steps.hint: Remember: if mid is bad, the first bad version could be mid or earlier. If mid is good, the first bad version must be after mid.
steps.expectedOutcome: Add the conditional logic and return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the complete binary search algorithm.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you handle both cases: when mid is bad and when mid is good.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: if (isBadVersion(mid)) { right = mid; } else { left = mid + 1; } After the loop, return left;

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient solution to find the first bad version using binary search. Remember: binary search works by repeatedly cutting the search space in half, making it much faster than checking every version. This pattern appears in many search problems where you need to find a boundary or transition point.
